name: South Sikkim
tagline: Big statues, tea, hot springs and village homestays
meta_description: South Sikkim (Namchi district) guide: Namchi, Ravangla, Temi tea, Char Dham, Buddha Park, homestays, festivals, best months and honest 2026 costs.
summary: South Sikkim, officially Namchi district, is the lowest, mildest and easiest part of Sikkim to travel. It holds the state's big pilgrim monuments at Namchi and Ravangla, Sikkim's only tea estate at Temi, winter hot springs and community homestays. No permits are needed for Indians, and October to May is the best time to go.
intro: South Sikkim runs from the Teesta and Rangeet valleys, at under 300 m around Melli and Jorethang, up to the 3,263 m summit of Maenam above Ravangla. A long ridge of Tendong and Maenam runs north to south through the middle of the district, dividing the Teesta side from the Rangeet side. Since December 2021 it has officially been Namchi district, after its headquarters town, but drivers, hotels and most travellers still say South Sikkim.

Most visitors come for the monuments. Namchi has two that face each other across the town: the Guru Padmasambhava statue on Samdruptse hill, completed in 2004, and the Char Dham complex at Solophok, opened in 2011 around a 108 ft Shiva. Ravangla, an hour north, adds the 130 ft Buddha of Tathagata Tsal, opened in 2013, and the Kagyu monastery of Ralang, founded in 1768. Together they make the district a pilgrim corridor for Buddhists and Hindus alike.

Beyond the monuments, South Sikkim is farm country. Temi, Sikkim's only tea estate, was planted in 1969 on a slope facing Kangchenjunga. Villages such as Kewzing, Borong and Yangang host guests in family homes, Borong has a winter hot spring on the Rangeet, and cardamom, ginger and oranges grow on the terraces. Kitam Bird Sanctuary protects low sal forest with wild peafowl, while Maenam and Tendong hold oak and rhododendron forest, so birders can climb from 400 m to over 3,000 m in a day.

The south is also the easiest district for first-timers, families and seniors. Altitudes are moderate, roads are good by Sikkim standards, there are no protected-area permits for Indian travellers and Namchi is under four hours from NJP or Bagdogra. Winters are cold but clear and seldom snowy, and the monsoon is wet but rarely closes the main towns for long. We send many guests here as a gentle start or end to a longer Sikkim trip.

story.title: Tendong Hill and the Lepcha flood
story.text: Look north from Namchi and the long, flat-topped ridge of Tendong fills the skyline. For the Lepcha, Sikkim's earliest known inhabitants, it is a sacred mountain. As recorded in the Wikipedia article on Tendong Lho Rum Faat and in festival reports, Lepcha tradition tells of a great flood in ancient times, when the Teesta and Rangeet rose until the valleys were drowned. The people climbed Tendong, which rose above the waters and kept them safe until the flood fell. The name is usually explained as the upraised horn, for the way the hill stood above the water. Each year on 8 August, Lepcha communities mark Tendong Lho Rum Faat, a prayer to the mountain, with rituals on and around the hill and, in some homes, a small model of Tendong built from nine stones. Sikkim observes the day as a state holiday. The story matters for travellers because it gives the district a centre older than any statue. Tendong, at about 2,600 m, is also one of the best half-day walks in South Sikkim: a forest trail of about 6 km from Damthang to a summit with views of Kangchenjunga to the north and the plains to the south. Walk it in October or November, and remember that, for many of the people around you, it is a holy place.

little_known.fact: At Mamley, just above Namchi, stromatolite-bearing dolomite of the Buxa Formation, Precambrian traces of early microbial life, is protected as a National Geological Monument by the Geological Survey of India.
little_known.source: Wikipedia: National Geological Monuments of India

little_known.fact: Temi Tea Garden was established in 1969 under Palden Thondup Namgyal, the last Chogyal of Sikkim, and remains the only tea estate in the state. Much of its tea is sold at auction in Kolkata.
Kitam Bird Sanctuary, declared on 3 February 2005 and covering about 6 sq km near the Rangeet, is the only protected area in Sikkim declared specifically as a bird sanctuary.
Former India football captain Bhaichung Bhutia was born at Tinkitam in South Sikkim, and Namchi's football stadium, the Bhaichung Stadium, is named after him.
Melli, the district's gateway on the Teesta, is split between two states: Melli Bazaar is in Kalimpong district of West Bengal and Melli across the bridge is in Namchi district of Sikkim.

highlights.title: Samdruptse and Char Dham, Namchi
highlights.text: Two hilltop monuments facing each other across Namchi: a gilded Guru Padmasambhava statue, about 135 ft tall and completed in 2004, and Siddhesvara Dham, opened in 2011, with a 108 ft Shiva and replicas of the four dhams. Both fit into one morning by car.

highlights.title: Buddha Park, Ravangla
highlights.text: Tathagata Tsal, opened in 2013, centres on a 130 ft copper-clad Buddha set against the Maenam ridge, with a museum inside the base. Ravangla, at about 2,050 m, is cooler than Namchi and the best base for Ralang, Maenam and the village homestays.

highlights.title: Temi Tea Garden
highlights.text: Sikkim's only tea estate, planted in 1969 on a slope facing Kangchenjunga between about 1,200 and 1,800 m. Walk among the bushes, buy organic orthodox tea at the estate and, in November, see wild cherry blossom along the road.

highlights.title: Ralang Monastery and its cham
highlights.text: A Kagyu monastery founded in 1768, rebuilt with a large new institute completed in 1995, 6 km from Ravangla. Its masked cham dances fall on Pang Lhabsol in August or September and on the 29th day of the 10th Tibetan month.

highlights.title: Village homestays and a hot spring
highlights.text: Kewzing runs a community homestay programme started in 2003, Yangang sits below the Bhaleydhunga rock, and Borong has a winter hot spring on the Rangeet. Expect about ₹1,200–2,500 per person a night with home-cooked meals.

highlights.title: Tendong Hill and Maenam
highlights.text: Two forested summits along the district's central ridge. Tendong, about 2,600 m, is a 6 km half-day walk sacred to the Lepcha. Maenam, 3,263 m, is a wildlife sanctuary and a long, steep day hike from Ravangla, with satyr tragopan calling in spring.

getting_there: There is no airport or railway in Namchi district. Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then drive about 96–100 km and 3.5–4 hours to Namchi via NH10 to Melli, where the road crosses the Teesta into Sikkim and climbs. NH10 closes after monsoon slides; the alternative for South Sikkim runs through Darjeeling district down to Jorethang, adding about an hour. Shared jeeps run from Siliguri to Namchi, Jorethang and Ravangla, roughly ₹300–400 a seat. From Gangtok, Namchi is about 78 km and Ravangla about 65 km, each around 3 hours, with shared jeeps through the day. Pakyong Airport has had no scheduled flights since June 2024, and the Sevoke–Rangpo railway is not open. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian nationals need no permit anywhere in Namchi district. Foreign nationals need the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, applied online through the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India since 12 January 2026, with approval usually in 24–48 hours; no extra protected-area permit is needed for South Sikkim as we understand it. Sikkim collects a ₹50 per tourist entry fee at hotels, valid 30 days, with under-fives exempt. Forest department rules and fees may apply in Maenam and Kitam sanctuaries. Check current status before you travel.
money: South Sikkim is one of the cheaper parts of the state. On a budget, shared jeeps cost about ₹250–400 a seat from Gangtok or Siliguri, clean budget rooms in Namchi or Ravangla run ₹1,500–2,500 and homestays ₹1,200–2,500 per person with meals; a 3-night trip from NJP can cost about ₹7,000–11,000 per person. Mid-range travellers with a private small car (about ₹3,500–4,500 a day) and good hotels or farmstays should budget ₹22,000–32,000 per person for 5–6 nights. Premium stays such as The Temi Bungalow or Sobralia's resort in Namchi push a comfortable week well above ₹50,000 per person. All figures are indicative; check current status before you travel.

months.summary: Cold, bright and quiet. Clear mornings give long views of the Kangchenjunga range from Samdruptse, Ravangla and Tendong, though afternoon haze builds. The Borong and Ralang hot springs are in season, with local families camping by the Rangeet. Mid-January brings the Maghe Sankranti mela at Jorethang, the district's biggest fair. Ravangla has frost most mornings and occasional light snow; pack proper winter layers.
months.tip: Book Namchi rooms early for mela week and pack thermals for Ravangla nights.

months.summary: Still cold at night but warming by day. Hot spring season continues at Borong, and the first rhododendrons can appear on Tendong late in the month. Maha Shivaratri often falls in February, bringing large crowds to Char Dham at Solophok. Losar, the Tibetan new year, falls in February in many years, with monastery rituals around Ravangla. A good month for quiet, cheaper stays.
months.tip: Check the date of Maha Shivaratri before visiting Char Dham, and avoid it if you dislike crowds.

months.summary: Spring arrives. Tree rhododendrons flower red and pink on Tendong and Maenam, Temi begins its first flush from late March, and birdsong fills the forests. Days are comfortable for walking and village stays, though mountain views are less reliable than in autumn. In years when Maha Shivaratri falls in early March, Char Dham is crowded on the day.
months.tip: Walk Tendong Hill early in the morning for the clearest light and the most birds.

months.summary: One of the best months for nature. Rhododendrons and magnolias flower in the upper forests, satyr tragopans call on Maenam and Temi's first flush continues. Kitam is still good for dawn birding before it gets hot. Afternoon clouds and occasional showers arrive, so plan walks and views for the morning. Comfortable for families and seniors.
months.tip: Start birding and hill walks at first light; by midday cloud usually gathers.

months.summary: Warm in Namchi and pleasant in Ravangla, which makes May popular with families escaping the plains during school holidays. Buddha Park and Ralang are busy, and Saga Dawa falls in some years. Pre-monsoon showers come most afternoons by late May, and haze often hides the high peaks. Book rooms early, especially in Ravangla.
months.tip: Book Ravangla hotels a month ahead for May school holidays.

months.summary: The monsoon reaches Sikkim and rain becomes daily. Forests turn deep green and visitor numbers fall, but cloud hides the mountains, forest paths are leech-prone and slides disrupt roads, including NH10 between Sevoke and Melli. The main towns and monuments stay open. Travel only with flexible plans and a buffer day.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day and check NH10 status each evening.

months.summary: The wettest month. Expect heavy rain most days, fog at Ravangla, leeches on every trail and occasional road closures. The hot springs are under the river and long walks are unwise. If you must travel, stay on main roads, base yourself in Namchi and focus on the monuments and covered sights, with monastery visits between showers.
months.tip: Carry a proper rain jacket and leech socks, and keep plans flexible.

months.summary: Still the monsoon, but culturally rich. Tendong Lho Rum Faat on 8 August sees Lepcha communities honour Tendong Hill, and in some years Pang Lhabsol, with cham at Ralang, falls in late August. Roads remain slow and slide-prone. Only come if a festival draws you, and travel with a local driver who checks conditions daily.
months.tip: Confirm festival dates locally; lunar dates shift every year.

months.summary: The monsoon eases through the month, waterfalls are at their fullest and the hills are green. Pang Lhabsol, with masked cham at Ralang Monastery, falls in September in most years. Late September brings the first clear mornings. Roads can still be affected by slides early in the month, so allow time.
months.tip: Book Ravangla rooms early for Pang Lhabsol week.

months.summary: The clear season begins. Washed skies bring Kangchenjunga views most mornings, Temi's autumn flush is under way and cardamom harvest fills the villages. Dasain, the biggest festival for Sikkim's Nepali-speaking families, falls in October in most years, followed by Tihar. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays make hotels busy, so book well ahead.
months.tip: Book early around Durga Puja and Diwali, when rooms fill and prices rise.

months.summary: Our pick of the year. The clearest skies of all, comfortable days, the end of the cardamom harvest and wild Himalayan cherry blossom along the Temi road. Tihar, the festival of lights, falls in late October or November. Ideal for village homestays, Tendong walks and photography, with cold but manageable nights in Ravangla.
months.tip: Be outside at sunrise: November mornings give the most reliable Kangchenjunga views.

months.summary: Crisp, clear and festive. Ralang holds its winter cham on the 29th day of the 10th Tibetan month, usually in December, and Losoong falls in some years. The hot spring season begins at Borong. Christmas and New Year bring weekend crowds to Ravangla from Siliguri and Gangtok. Nights are cold, so pack warm layers.
months.tip: Check the Tibetan calendar for Ralang's winter cham dates before booking.

faqs.a: Yes, especially for families, seniors, pilgrims and first-time visitors. South Sikkim has the state's biggest monuments at Namchi and Ravangla, Sikkim's only tea estate at Temi, easy village homestays and mild weather. It needs no permits for Indians and is under four hours from NJP. Two to four nights suit most trips.

Namchi district is the official name, since December 2021, of what was South Sikkim district. Its headquarters is Namchi. The district covers Namchi, Ravangla, Temi, Jorethang, Melli and the villages around them. Travellers, drivers and hotels still widely use the name South Sikkim.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Samdruptse and Char Dham in Namchi, Buddha Park and Ralang Monastery near Ravangla, Temi Tea Garden, Tendong Hill and Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary for walks, Kitam for birds, and the village homestays of Kewzing, Borong and Yangang. Jorethang's mid-January fair is worth timing a trip around.

faqs.q: How many days do we need for South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Two nights cover the highlights: one in Namchi for Samdruptse and Char Dham, one in Ravangla for Buddha Park and Ralang, with Temi on the way. Four nights let you add a village homestay at Kewzing or Borong, a Tendong walk or a dawn at Kitam. Many guests combine it with Gangtok and Pelling.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit South Sikkim?
faqs.a: October to December for clear skies and mountain views, and March to May for flowers, tea and birds. January and February are cold but clear, with hot springs in season. June to September is the monsoon: green and quiet, but cloudy, leech-prone and subject to road slides.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit. Foreign nationals need the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, applied online through the e-FRRO portal since January 2026; no extra protected-area permit is needed for South Sikkim as we understand it. Hotels collect Sikkim's ₹50 entry fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do we reach South Sikkim from NJP or Bagdogra?
faqs.a: By road: about 96–100 km and 3.5–4 hours to Namchi via NH10 and Melli, for roughly ₹4,500–6,500 by reserved car, or by shared jeep from Siliguri for about ₹300–400 a seat. When NH10 is closed, vehicles go through Darjeeling district to Jorethang. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is South Sikkim good for a family trip with elderly parents?
faqs.a: Very. Altitudes are moderate, about 1,500 m at Namchi and 2,050 m at Ravangla, so altitude sickness is rarely a concern. The main monuments have paved paths, hotels with lifts exist in Namchi, and drives between sights are short. Namchi has a district hospital. Pack warm clothes for winter nights.

faqs.q: Does it snow in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Rarely, and only lightly. Ravangla and the summits of Tendong and Maenam can see a dusting on cold days between late December and February in some years. Namchi almost never gets snow. If snow is your goal, plan for North Sikkim or Tsomgo Lake in East Sikkim instead.
